title: #66 Check Students Are Listening to Each Other
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton extends his recurring concern about student listening from teacher-to-student to student-to-student attention, arguing that classroom culture often trains students to switch off the moment a question isn't directed at them. He illustrates this with a Venn diagram exchange: a student, Mollie, explains why she placed her initials in a particular region, and when the teacher immediately asks another student, Tom, to explain Mollie's reasoning, Tom's blank "What?" reveals he hadn't been listening because the moment wasn't about him. Barton says this pattern is pervasive -- when he randomly asks other students to repeat what a peer just said, they almost always cannot -- and argues it's a problem on two levels: pedagogically, because teachers often build their next move on the false assumption that everyone heard the prior answer, and more broadly, because it normalises a habit of tuning out other people's speech. His proposed fix is straightforward: regularly and unpredictably ask students to repeat or build on what a classmate just said, and hold them accountable when they can't.
points: The core diagnostic Barton uses -- asking random students to repeat what a peer just said -- almost always exposes that students were not listening to each other, only to the teacher.

The Mollie/Tom Venn diagram exchange shows the pattern concretely: a student assumes a question addressed to a classmate isn't their responsibility to track, so they disengage the instant attention shifts away from them.

Teachers often build their next instructional move on the unverified assumption that the whole class heard a given student's answer, which the tip identifies as a hidden reliability problem in responsive teaching.
Barton frames the habit as a societal concern as well as a pedagogical one, arguing that routinely tuning out peers in the classroom risks normalising the same habit outside it.
quotes: Regular readers will know that I am obsessed with the fact that many students are not listening to us as much as we hope they are.
But if students may not listen to us, they almost certainly do not listen to each other.
One of my favourite things to do after a student has answered a question is to ask three other students at random what that student just said. They almost always cannot.
This is clearly a problem from a learning perspective, especially if we base our next teacher move on the assumption everyone has heard what that student said.
It is also not great from a societal perspective as we help breed a cohort of young people who switch off whenever someone else speaks.

The solution is relatively straightforward: regularly check students are listening to each other by asking them to repeat - or build upon - what another student has said, and then hold them to account if they cannot.
